name: German
summary: German is a West Germanic, fusional language written in the Latin alphabet with ä, ö, ü and ß, in which every noun is capitalized. Its grammar lives in the noun phrase: three grammatical genders, four cases carried mostly by articles and adjectives, and adjective endings that change with the determiner (strong / weak / mixed). Its syntax is built around the verb's position – second in main clauses, first in yes/no questions, last in subordinate clauses – with the sentence bracket of modal + infinitive, auxiliary + participle and separable particles. Its lexicon splits several everyday meanings into separate words (gehen / fahren, kennen / wissen, als / wenn / wann, zu / nach / in) and colours speech with modal particles and the du / Sie choice; three national standards (Germany, Austria, Switzerland) coexist. It has no lexical tone, no numeral classifiers, no grammatical aspect, no dual and no honorific verb forms.

phenomena.title: Latin alphabet with ä, ö, ü and ß
phenomena.alsoNote: Latin alphabet with umlaut vowels as letters of their own: et ä ö ü, fi/sv ä ö, hu/tr/az ö ü. ß is German only; other Latin-script languages share the basic alphabet but not the umlaut letters.
phenomena.what: German is written from left to right in one script, the Latin alphabet: the 26 basic letters plus the umlaut letters ä, ö, ü and the letter ß (Eszett), with spaces between words. Every vowel is written with a letter. Umlauts are separate vowels, not accents: Mutter (mother) and Mütter (mothers) are different words. Without these keys they are written ae, oe, ue and ss (Maedchen, Strasse) – acceptable in e-mails, wrong in careful writing. Old print and some signs use Fraktur, a broken typeface of the same alphabet.

phenomena.title: One shape per letter: no joining, no positional forms
phenomena.what: Each letter has one printed shape, a capital and a small one, wherever it stands in the word. Printed letters are not joined and have no special initial, medial or final forms. ß is a letter of its own, not a final form of s; the long ſ of old blackletter print is no longer used.

phenomena.title: ß or ss – and the spelling reform
phenomena.alsoNote: The ß/ss rule after long/short vowels is German only (Swiss Standard German writes ss throughout).
phenomena.what: ß is written after a long vowel or a diphthong, ss after a short vowel (rule of the 1996 reform): heißen, Straße, aß – but dass, essen, isst. The same verb can switch: essen (short e) → er isst (short i) → er aß (long a). Switzerland and Liechtenstein never use ß (Strasse, heissen). Since 2017 a capital ẞ exists for all-caps text (STRASSE or STRAẞE). The reform of 1996 also replaced daß by dass and keeps three equal consonants in compounds (Brennnessel, Schifffahrt); older texts show the old spellings.

phenomena.title: Capital letters for every noun – and for polite Sie
phenomena.what: Every noun starts with a capital letter, also nouns made from other words (das Essen, das Gute, beim Kochen), while ich is small. The polite pronoun Sie and its forms Ihnen, Ihr are capitalized too; sie/ihr in small letters mean she, they, her, their, you (plural). So the capital decides the meaning of several homographs: morgen (tomorrow) – der Morgen (the morning), essen (to eat) – das Essen (the food, the meal), ihnen (to them) – Ihnen (to you, polite).

phenomena.title: Punctuation: commas by syntax, „…“, decimal comma, ordinal dot
phenomena.alsoNote: Czech has the same set: commas before every subordinate clause, „…“ quotes, decimal comma, ordinal dot. Partly: pl, hu, sr (ordinal dot, low–high quotes), ru (syntactic commas, decimal comma, «…» quotes).
phenomena.what: Commas follow the grammar, not the breath: every subordinate clause is separated by a comma (Ich weiß, dass er kommt), also relative clauses and most infinitive groups with um … zu. Quotation marks are „…“ (low–high) or »…«. Numbers use a decimal comma and a thousands point (1,5 · 1.000), and a dot after a number makes it an ordinal: am 3. Mai = am dritten Mai.

phenomena.title: Long and short vowels
phenomena.what: Vowel length distinguishes words: Staat (state) – Stadt (city), ihn (him) – in (in), Beet (flower bed) – Bett (bed). Spelling gives hints: a doubled vowel, h after the vowel and ie mark a long vowel; a doubled consonant marks a short one. Short vowels are also more open (in [ɪ] vs ihn [iː]).

phenomena.title: No lexical tone: pitch never changes a word
phenomena.what: German has no lexical tone: a word keeps its meaning whatever pitch it is said on, and there is no tone to write. Pitch carries intonation only – the sentence type, focus and attitude: a falling end for statements and question-word questions, a rising end for yes/no questions, a high pitch on the word in focus. Words are kept apart by vowels, consonants, vowel length and stress instead (Staat – Stadt, ˈumfahren – umˈfahren).

phenomena.title: The vowels ö, ü (and ä)
phenomena.what: ö and ü are front rounded vowels: ü [yː, ʏ] has the tongue position of i with rounded lips, ö [øː, œ] that of e with rounded lips; each has a long and a short variant. Lip rounding alone separates words: Kiste (box) – Küste (coast), lesen (read) – lösen (solve). ä is an open e [ɛ, ɛː].
phenomena.record: Pronunciation of the lemma (IPA).

phenomena.title: Unstressed e: the weak vowel schwa
phenomena.what: e in unstressed endings and prefixes is a weak central vowel [ə] (bitte, gesagt, Tage), and in -en, -el, -em after a consonant it often disappears, leaving a syllabic consonant: haben [ˈhaːbn̩], Tafel [ˈtaːfl̩]. The ending -er is the vowel [ɐ] (Lehrer [ˈleːʁɐ]). Other vowels keep their quality when unstressed (Kaˈffee, Ziˈtrone) and are only shorter.

phenomena.title: Two sounds of ch: ich and ach
phenomena.alsoNote: Greek χ is [ç] before e/i and [x] elsewhere (the following vowel decides, in German the preceding one). Partly: ru х/хь; nl, he, ar, cy, es have only the ach-sound.
phenomena.what: ch has two sounds chosen by the vowel before it: after a, o, u and au it is a fricative at the back of the mouth, velar [x] or uvular [χ] (Bach, Buch, auch – the ach-sound); after all other vowels, after consonants and in -chen it is the palatal [ç] (ich, Milch, Mädchen – the ich-sound). The two never distinguish words. At the start of a word ch is [k] or [ç] (Chor, China) and [ʃ] in French loans (Chef). The ending -ig is [ɪç] in the standard of Germany (zwanzig), [ɪk] in the south and Austria.

phenomena.title: r and l; the uvular r
phenomena.what: r and l are separate sounds that distinguish words (Rand – Land, Reise – leise). The standard r is uvular – a fricative or approximant [ʁ] made with the back of the tongue against the uvula, near the ach-sound; a tongue-tip trill [r] is usual in parts of the south, in Austria and in Switzerland. After a long vowel r becomes the vowel [ɐ̯] (der [deːɐ̯], Uhr [uːɐ̯]). l is always a clear [l].

phenomena.title: Final devoicing
phenomena.what: b, d, g, s and v at the end of a word or syllable are pronounced voiceless – [p, t, k, s, f] – but the spelling keeps the letter of the voiced sound. Add an ending and the voiced sound comes back: Tag [taːk] – Tage [ˈtaːɡə], Hund [hʊnt] – Hunde [ˈhʊndə]. So Rad (wheel) and Rat (advice) sound the same.
phenomena.record: Pronunciation of the lemma (IPA).

phenomena.title: Voiced and voiceless consonants
phenomena.what: Plosives and fricatives come in voiceless–voiced pairs that distinguish words: p – b (Pass – Bass), t – d (Tank – Dank), k – g (Kasse – Gasse), s – z, written s before a vowel (reißen [s] – reisen [z]), f – v, written f/v – w (Fall – Wall). In the south, in Austria and in Switzerland b, d, g and s are often voiceless but weak and unaspirated, so the pairs are told apart by strength and breath. The contrast holds only before a vowel: at the end of a syllable all are voiceless (final devoicing).
phenomena.gap: The overview mentions final devoicing only; an `ipa` parameter per word and a pronunciation page with minimal pairs.

phenomena.title: No aspiration contrast
phenomena.what: Aspiration never distinguishes words. p, t, k are aspirated at the start of a stressed syllable ([pʰ, tʰ, kʰ]: Pass, Tag, Kuss), less after s or sch and at the end of a word, but this is automatic. b, d, g are never aspirated. Where b, d, g are voiceless (southern speech), the puff of air on p, t, k is what keeps the pairs apart.

phenomena.title: No pharyngeal or emphatic consonants
phenomena.what: German has no consonants made in the pharynx and no pharyngealised (emphatic) consonants. h is a plain breath [h] (Haus) and is silent after a vowel, where it only marks length (sehen, Kuh); the farthest-back consonants are ch [x, χ] and the uvular r [ʁ]. t, s, d have one variant each.

phenomena.title: No ejectives, implosives or clicks
phenomena.what: Every German consonant is made with air pushed out from the lungs: there are no ejectives, no implosives and no clicks. The clicks people make (tsk for disapproval, a tongue click to call a horse) are sounds outside the word system.

examples.note: p, t, k: plain stops from the lungs, aspirated at the start
a click of disapproval – never part of a word

phenomena.gap: Say it in the overview for learners whose languages have ejectives, implosives or clicks: German stops are plain.

phenomena.title: No retroflex consonants
phenomena.what: t, d, n, l are made with the tongue tip at the ridge behind the upper teeth (alveolar), and sch [ʃ] is a rounded post-alveolar hiss; no consonant is made with the tongue tip curled back. rt, rd, rn and rl are two sounds each – the r is uvular or turns into a vowel after the vowel – never merged into one retroflex sound.

examples.note: r + t: two sounds, no retroflex

phenomena.gap: Say it on a pronunciation page for learners whose languages have retroflex consonants.

phenomena.title: No ‘th’ sounds
phenomena.what: German has no dental fricatives [θ, ð]. The letters th are rare and stand for a plain t (Theater, Thema, Apotheke); in loanwords many speakers replace a th sound by s, z, t or d.

examples.note: th is t in every native and Greek-derived word

phenomena.gap: Say it on a pronunciation page: th is read t.

phenomena.title: No hard and soft consonant pairs
phenomena.what: Consonants do not come in hard and soft (palatalised) pairs: a consonant before i or e is the same sound as before a, o, u. Only ch changes with the vowel before it ([ç] after front vowels, [x] after back ones), and that never distinguishes words. j [j] is a consonant of its own (ja, Jahr).

phenomena.gap: Say it on a pronunciation page for learners whose languages have palatalised consonants.

phenomena.title: No nasal vowels
phenomena.what: German vowels are oral; n and m after a vowel are always pronounced as consonants (Bank [baŋk], Kinder, kommen). Nasal vowels occur only in some French loanwords, and many speakers replace them by a vowel + [ŋ]: Restaurant [ʁɛstoˈʁãː] or [ʁɛstoˈʁaŋ], Balkon [balˈkɔŋ] or [balˈkoːn].

phenomena.title: No long (double) consonants
phenomena.what: German has no long consonants. A doubled letter (kommen, Mitte, Bett, essen) is pronounced as one short consonant; it only shows that the vowel before it is short. So Mitte and Miete differ in the vowel (short [ɪ] – long [iː]), not in the t. Only across a word or compound boundary can two equal consonants meet (Schifffahrt, mit Tom).

phenomena.title: No vowel harmony
phenomena.what: Endings and suffixes keep their own vowels whatever the vowels of the stem: -en, -er, -e, -chen, -in, -ung, -heit are the same after front or back, rounded or unrounded stem vowels. The vowels of a word do not have to match.

phenomena.title: Consonant clusters
phenomena.what: A syllable can begin with up to three consonants and end with up to four or five: Strumpf, sprechen, Pflanze, Herbst, du schimpfst. Endings add more consonants (-st, -t, -s), and no vowel is inserted to break a cluster up: du kämpfst, des Obsts, du hilfst.

examples.note: sock: three consonants at each end

phenomena.gap: Nothing in the course practises clusters; an `ipa` parameter per word and a pronunciation page.

phenomena.title: No consonant mutation or gradation
phenomena.what: The first consonant of a word never changes with the word before it, and stems do not alternate between strong and weak consonant grades: Haus stays Haus in das Haus, mein Haus, in meinem Haus. The sound alternations German does have are final devoicing (Tag [k] – Tage [ɡ]) and the vowel changes of umlaut and ablaut.

examples.text: das Haus · mein Haus · in meinem Haus
examples.note: the noun's first consonant is fixed

phenomena.title: Letter–sound rules and the glottal stop
phenomena.alsoNote: The letter–sound correspondences (st/sp = [ʃt]/[ʃp], z = [ts], w = [v], ei = [aɪ̯], ie = [iː]) are German; nl shares some (ie, sch) but differs in most.
phenomena.what: German spelling is regular once a few rules are known: st and sp at the start of a word or stem are [ʃt], [ʃp]; z is [ts]; v is usually [f] and w is [v]; ei is [aɪ̯] but ie is [iː]; eu and äu are [ɔʏ̯]; s before a vowel is [z]; pf is one sound [p͡f]; r after a vowel and in -er becomes a vowel [ɐ]. phenomena.title: Word stress: stem, prefixes, loanwords
phenomena.alsoNote: Dutch has the same system: stem-initial stress in native words, stressed separable vs unstressed inseparable prefixes, compounds stressed on the first part. Partly: en, sv (Germanic stem stress, different loanword and prefix patterns).
phenomena.what: Stress is never marked in writing. Native words stress the first syllable of the stem (ˈLehrer, ˈkaufen). Separable prefixes are stressed (ˈankommen), inseparable ones never (verˈlassen) – stress tells the two verb types apart. Compounds stress their first part (ˈKühlschrank). Many loanwords keep a final stress (Caˈfé, Büˈro, Universiˈtät); some words differ by country: Kaffee is ˈKaffee in Germany, Kaˈffee in Austria.

phenomena.title: Three grammatical genders
phenomena.what: Every noun is masculine (der), feminine (die) or neuter (das). For people and many animals the gender mostly follows sex (der Mann, die Frau, der Hahn, die Henne), but for most nouns it is purely grammatical and is learned with the noun (der Löffel, die Gabel, das Messer – spoon, fork, knife); some person nouns break the link too: das Mädchen (girl) and das Kind are neuter, die Person is feminine for a man as well. The gender chooses the article, dieser, the pronoun (der Tisch → er) and the adjective ending.

examples.text: der Tisch · die Tür · das Fenster
der Löffel · die Gabel · das Messer

phenomena.title: Clues to the gender: suffixes, meaning classes, compounds
phenomena.what: Some endings decide the gender: -ung, -heit, -keit, -schaft, -ion, -in are feminine; -chen, -lein neuter; -ling, -ismus masculine. Meaning classes help too: days, months and seasons are masculine (der Montag, der Mai, der Sommer). Most nouns in -e are feminine, with important exceptions (der Junge, der Name, der Käse, das Auge). A compound takes the gender of its last part.

phenomena.what: Some nouns exist with two genders, and each gender is a different word with its own meaning and often its own plural. The article is the only thing that tells them apart in writing.

phenomena.title: Plural classes – and the dative plural -n
phenomena.alsoNote: Swedish also has several lexical plural classes, some with umlaut (bok – böcker, man – män). Neither sv nor any other language has the dative plural -n. Partly: nl (mainly -en / -s); ru, el, la, ar learn plurals by declension class or pattern.
phenomena.what: Every countable noun has a plural, and it is used after every number above one (zwei Tische). There is no single plural ending: -e (Tische), umlaut + -e (Stühle), -er with umlaut (Bücher), -(e)n (Frauen, Lampen), -nen after -in (Lehrerinnen), -s (Handys) and no ending, sometimes with umlaut only (Zimmer, Mütter). The plural is learned with the noun (der Stuhl, -¨e). The plural article is die for all genders, and ein has no plural. In the dative plural every noun ends in -n unless the plural already ends in -n or -s (mit den Kindern, but mit den Frauen, den Handys).

examples.text: der Tisch – die Tische; der Stuhl – die Stühle
das Buch – die Bücher; die Lampe – die Lampen
das Handy – die Handys; das Zimmer – die Zimmer; die Mutter – die Mütter
die Frauen → mit den Frauen; die Handys → mit den Handys

phenomena.title: No dual
phenomena.what: Number has two values, singular and plural; two of something takes the ordinary plural (zwei Bücher, beide Hände), and pronouns and verbs have no dual forms. Pairs are named with words: beide (both), ein Paar (a pair), zu zweit (as two).

examples.note: we two go: a plural pronoun and verb, beide adds the number

model.other: Comparison notes (D18): fn.plural.noun notes (ar, he, iu) and fn.numerals note (iu).

phenomena.title: Different plurals for different meanings
phenomena.alsoNote: ru листы/листья, зубы/зубья; nl bladen/bladeren; it bracci/braccia, ossi/ossa – one singular, two plurals for two meanings. en has only relics (brothers / brethren).
phenomena.what: A few nouns have two meanings with two different plurals; the singular is the same word: die Bank – Banken (banks) / Bänke (benches), die Mutter – Mütter (mothers) / Muttern (nuts for bolts), das Wort – Wörter (single words) / Worte (sayings).

examples.text: die Bank → die Banken / die Bänke
die Mutter → die Mütter / die Muttern
das Wort → die Wörter / die Worte

phenomena.record: features.plurals: [{form, pattern, senses, note?}] – every plural of a noun, each tied to the profile senses it belongs to; a meaning in no item has no plural; none for mass and plural-only nouns.

model.other: Every noun states its plurals: de:Bank Banken (s1) / Bänke (s2), de:Mutter Mütter / Muttern, de:Glas Gläser and Glas after numbers (zwei Glas Wein), de:Uhr Uhren (clock) / acht Uhr, de:Wasser Wasser / Wässer, de:Land Länder for the country senses only; the word card shows each meaning with its plural (langcore meanings()). The N;*;PL cells of forms hold the first plural.

phenomena.title: Umlaut as a grammatical signal
phenomena.alsoNote: Swedish uses umlaut in noun plurals (man – män, bok – böcker) and in comparison (stor – större), not in verbs. en keeps relics only (man – men, foot – feet, old – elder).
phenomena.what: Umlaut – a change of the stem vowel a → ä, o → ö, u → ü, au → äu inside the word – marks grammar in many places: noun plurals, comparison, the du/er present of some strong verbs, female nouns, diminutives and the Konjunktiv II. It often goes together with an ending (Buch – Bücher, alt – älter) but can be the only sign (Mutter – Mütter).

examples.text: fahren – du fährst; laufen – er läuft
Koch – Köchin; Haus – Häuschen; hatte – hätte

model.other: All umlaut forms are stored as forms; the parameters name the umlaut where it is a pattern: plurals pattern “umlaut + -e / -er / only”, presentChange a>ä / au>äu, ADJ comparison “umlaut”; traps in fn.plural.noun, fn.comparison and fn.imperative.

phenomena.gap: No overview page that ties the umlaut together; no exercise sorts words by these patterns yet.

phenomena.title: Four cases, shown mostly on the article
phenomena.alsoNote: Four cases carried mostly by the article and adjective, with little change on the noun, is German only. Partly: el (article declines for three cases, noun changes too), sq (inflected linking articles).
phenomena.what: German has four cases – nominative, accusative, dative, genitive. They are marked by endings, but the noun itself changes little (dative plural -n, genitive -s, weak nouns -n); the case is carried mostly by the endings of the article, the pronoun and the adjective. Only the masculine singular shows the accusative (der → den).

examples.text: der Tisch – den Tisch – dem Tisch – des Tisches
mit dem Bus, in der Küche

model.other: DET/PRON/NOUN/ADJ paradigms in language.json have all four cases; bank tokens are tagged with the case and checked against the forms.

phenomena.gap: The genitive is stored but never taught (only während + GEN in fn.prep.time); the `analyze` and `parse` exercises (form → case) are not implemented.

phenomena.title: One subject case for every verb
phenomena.what: The subject is in the nominative and the verb agrees with it, whether the verb has an object or not: Der Mann schläft. Der Mann sieht den Hund. The direct object is in the accusative (den Hund). So the one who acts on something and the one who just sleeps, comes or falls are marked the same way. The passive makes the object the nominative subject (Der Hund wird gesehen).

examples.note: subject of a verb without object: nominative
subject of a verb with object: the same nominative; object accusative

model.other: Comparison notes (D18): fn.overview notes (hi, iu) and fn.case.basic notes (hi, mr, iu: ergative subjects).

phenomena.title: The genitive: -s/-es, Annas, von + dative
phenomena.what: Masculine and neuter nouns add -s or -es in the genitive singular (des Tisches, des Brots / des Brotes); feminine nouns add nothing (der Mutter). The genitive phrase normally follows the noun it belongs to (das Haus des Vaters); names take -s without an apostrophe and stand before it (Annas Buch). Spoken German often replaces the genitive with von + dative, and a few prepositions take the genitive (während, wegen, trotz).

model.other: N;GEN;SG is required for every noun and shown by principalParts (des Tisches); formsAlt holds alternants (Brots/Brotes, Fischs, Arzts); wer → wessen in fn.question.wh; während + GEN in fn.prep.time (3 bank sentences).

phenomena.gap: A genitive lesson (possession, von + dative in speech, genitive prepositions); genitive cells for adjectives (missing in language.json ADJ cells).

phenomena.title: No construct state or linker
phenomena.what: When one noun belongs to another, the possessed noun keeps its full form and its own article: das Haus des Vaters (the father's house), die Tür des Hauses. Nothing links the two nouns and the head noun does not change its shape; the possessor is marked by the genitive, by von + dative, or the two nouns form a compound (das Vaterhaus).

examples.note: the head noun keeps its article; the possessor is in the genitive
a compound instead of two nouns

model.other: Comparison notes (D18): fn.possessive notes (ar, he: construct state; fa: ezafe).

phenomena.title: Weak masculine nouns (n-declension)
phenomena.alsoNote: The weak (n-) declension class is German; noun declension classes as such are familiar from ru, el, la and others.
phenomena.what: A group of masculine nouns – mostly persons and animals in -e, and loan nouns in -ent, -ist, -ant – take -(e)n in every case except the nominative singular. A few mixed nouns add -s in the genitive as well (der Name, des Namens). Herr is weak in the singular (Herrn) and takes -en in the plural (Herren).

examples.text: der Junge – den Jungen – dem Jungen – des Jungen
der Student → mit dem Studenten; der Polizist → beim Polizisten
der Herr – den Herrn – die Herren

phenomena.record: features.declension: strong | weak | mixed | feminine | adjectival (the singular declension; plural-only nouns have none).

phenomena.gap: Drills do not yet pick the weak nouns from declension (fn.case still lists them by hand); Herr is not in the course.

phenomena.title: Nouns that decline like adjectives
phenomena.what: Nouns made from adjectives and participles keep adjective endings: der Verwandte but ein Verwandter, die Verwandten but Verwandte. Common ones: der/die Deutsche, Bekannte, Erwachsene, Angestellte, Verwandte.

examples.note: weak after der, strong after ein

phenomena.gap: No function or generator for adjectival nouns.

phenomena.title: Plural-only and mass nouns
phenomena.what: Some nouns exist only in the plural (die Leute, die Eltern, die Großeltern, die Ferien); one parent is ein Elternteil, one person eine Person. Mass nouns (Obst, Milch, Zucker, Fleisch) have no ordinary plural; their plurals mean sorts (Weine, Käse).

examples.text: die Leute, die Eltern, die Ferien

model.other: language.json paradigms NOUN.sgt and NOUN.plt; principalParts shows ‘plural only’; gender_article skips class plt; validator does not ask gender for plt.

phenomena.title: No singulative
phenomena.what: Nouns have no special form for one item of a collective or a mass. A countable noun is singular by default (eine Tomate – Tomaten). A mass or collective noun is counted with a measure noun or a different word for the single item: ein Stück Seife, eine Scheibe Brot, das Obst – ein Apfel, das Vieh – ein Rind.

examples.note: the singular is the basic form
a piece of soap: one item of a mass by a measure noun
fruit (collective) – an apple: a separate word

model.other: Comparison notes (D18): fn.plural.noun note (ar).

phenomena.title: Measure nouns stay singular: zwei Glas Wasser
phenomena.alsoNote: Masculine/neuter measure nouns staying singular after a number is German. nl and sv share the juxtaposition without a word for ‘of’ (een kop koffie, en kopp kaffe).
phenomena.what: After a number, masculine and neuter nouns of measure stay in the singular: zwei Glas Wasser, drei Stück Kuchen, zehn Euro; feminine ones take the plural (zwei Tassen Kaffee). The measured thing follows directly, with no word for “of”. In ordering, a drink itself counts as a portion: Zwei Bier, bitte.

examples.note: Glas stays singular (zwei Gläser Wasser also correct)

model.other: features.plurals records the unchanged form after numbers on the course words that are units: de:Glas (zwei Glas Wein) and de:Uhr (acht Uhr); formsAlt of de:Tee and de:Bier accept Tee / Bier as plural; fn.overview forYou(de) mentions “zwei Glas Bier”.

phenomena.gap: No `measure` flag on other unit nouns (Kilo, Liter, Stück are not course words yet) and no lesson point with bank sentences.

phenomena.title: No numeral classifiers
phenomena.what: A numeral stands directly before the noun: zwei Bücher, drei Katzen, vier Autos. No classifier word is chosen by the shape or kind of the thing counted. Measure nouns are needed only for masses and portions (zwei Glas Wasser, ein Stück Kuchen, eine Flasche Wein), and they are ordinary nouns with gender and number.

examples.note: a measure noun only for a mass

model.other: Comparison notes (D18): fn.numerals notes (zh, vi, ja, ko).

phenomena.title: Female nouns in -in and gender-fair forms
phenomena.what: Most nouns for people have a female form in -in (plural -innen), often with umlaut: der Lehrer – die Lehrerin, der Arzt – die Ärztin, der Koch – die Köchin. Some pairs use another word (der Krankenpfleger – die Krankenschwester). In job sentences the form follows the person: Er ist Koch. Sie ist Köchin. For mixed groups many texts now name both forms (Lehrerinnen und Lehrer), use participles (Studierende) or a written sign (Lehrer*innen).

examples.text: der Lehrer → die Lehrerin → die Lehrerinnen
der Arzt → die Ärztin; der Koch → die Köchin

phenomena.record: pair: the lexeme id of the female / male counterpart.

model.other: Each job / person concept has two lexemes (de:Arzt, de:Ärztin …), contrasted on the axis “sex of the person”; features.compound names the derivation (Ärztin: derived, Arzt + -in).

phenomena.gap: A `pair` link would apply to person nouns only (German declares parameters per part of speech, so it is not declared); a ‘make the female form’ drill (umlaut traps: Ärztin, Köchin, Anwältin).

phenomena.title: Diminutives -chen and -lein
phenomena.what: -chen and -lein make a small or dear thing; the result is always neuter and usually takes umlaut. Regions have their own: -le (Swabia), -li (Switzerland), -erl (Bavaria, Austria: Vogerlsalat). Mädchen itself is an old diminutive (of Magd).

examples.note: Austrian -erl, a variant of Feldsalat in the course

phenomena.record: diminutive: the diminutive form (or none).

model.other: Only as a gender cue (fn.noun.gender: -chen, -lein → das).

phenomena.gap: A `diminutive` field or derivation links; regional suffixes in variants.

phenomena.title: Compounds written as one word
phenomena.what: Compounding is the main way of making new nouns, and compounds can be long (Haustür, Kühlschranktür, Krankenversicherungskarte). The last part is the head and gives the gender and the plural; the first parts narrow it down. A linking element often stands between the parts (-s-, -n-, -en-, -er-). Compounds are written as one word, without spaces, and stressed on the first part.
phenomena.record: features.compound: [{part, role: modifier | head, linker?}], or none with the reason (a simple word, derived: Freund + -in, two words: Rote Bete).

model.other: Every noun states its parts (105 compounds: Blume-n-kohl, Geburt-s-tag, Kirsch(−e)-tomate, Schlange-n-haar-gurke) or why it is not a compound; weekday names are explained as historical compounds. fn.noun.gender callout “Compounds: the last part decides”. §6.2 lists `compound_split`, not implemented yet.

phenomena.gap: The compound_split exercise (split, find the gender from the head) is not implemented; adjectives and verbs (hellblau, zurückkommen) have no compound parameter.

phenomena.title: Derivation: -ung, -er, -heit, -lich, un- …
phenomena.what: New words are made with suffixes and prefixes, each with a fixed meaning and often a fixed gender: -ung (action → feminine noun), -er (doer), -heit/-keit (quality), -lich/-ig (adjectives), un- (negation).
phenomena.record: family: derived from / derivatives (lexeme ids).

model.other: Only the etymology text of each profile.

phenomena.gap: A word-family field (like ar/he root families) and a family exercise.

phenomena.title: No root-and-pattern morphology
phenomena.what: Words are built from a stem by adding prefixes, suffixes and other stems; meanings are not carried by a skeleton of consonants filled with vowel patterns. Strong verbs and some related nouns do change the stem vowel (singen – sang – gesungen – der Gesang; trinken – trank – das Getränk), but these vowel series belong to a closed list of old verbs and are learned word by word; they are never applied to new words.

examples.note: a closed ablaut series, learned with the verb
a word family built with affixes on an unchanged stem

model.other: Comparison notes (D18): fn.overview notes (ar, he).

phenomena.title: No reduplication
phenomena.what: Doubling a word or a part of it is not a grammatical process: it makes neither plurals, nor intensity, nor repeated or spread-out action. Plurality is shown by endings (Häuser), intensity by sehr or a prefix-like first part (sehr groß, riesengroß), repetition by immer wieder. Only a few expressive words look doubled (Wirrwarr, Mischmasch, Zickzack), and repeating a word for emphasis (ganz, ganz toll) is a matter of style.

examples.note: houses: the plural by an ending, never by doubling
huge: intensity by a first part
he knocks again and again: repetition by an adverb

model.other: Comparison notes (D18): fn.overview note (zh).

phenomena.title: Any word can become a noun
phenomena.what: An infinitive becomes a neuter noun (das Essen, das Kochen), an adjective a noun with adjective endings (das Gute, etwas Neues); both are capitalized. beim + infinitive means ‘while doing’.
phenomena.gap: A grammar point and bank sentences; lexemes for the common ones (das Essen).

phenomena.title: Definite and indefinite articles that decline
phenomena.alsoNote: Greek articles also decline for gender, number and case, and ένας/μία/ένα is the numeral ‘one’. fr, es, it, pt articles vary for gender and number only.
phenomena.what: German has a definite article der/die/das and an indefinite article ein/eine/ein, both separate words before the noun; ein is the same word as the numeral ‘one’. Both change for gender, number and case – sixteen cells with only six forms, so one form has several readings (der = masculine nominative, feminine dative or genitive, genitive plural). ein has no plural: ein Buch → Bücher.

model.other: DET.def / DET.indef paradigms (16 / 12 cells) in language.json; de:der and de:ein; transform Definiteness variants (14 bank sentences).

phenomena.title: Endings that carry several meanings at once
phenomena.what: Grammar is shown mostly by endings at the end of the word, and one ending carries several meanings together: the -m of dem means dative + singular + masculine or neuter; the -st of du kommst means 2nd person + singular + present. The same ending can mean different things in different words (-er: plural in Kinder, comparative in größer, doer in Lehrer, adjective ending in ein großer Tisch), and stems change inside the word too (Mann – Männer, sprechen – spricht). Forms are therefore learned in tables. Prefixes are fewer: ge- of the participle (ge-kauf-t) and derivational prefixes such as be-, ver-, un-.

phenomena.title: Possessives: the owner picks the word, the noun picks the ending
phenomena.alsoNote: Owner chooses the stem, owned noun the ending: rare. Partly: sq (i tij / e saj); en, nl, sv mark only the owner's sex (his/her); fr, es, it agree only with the owned noun.
phenomena.what: mein, dein, sein, ihr, unser, euer, Ihr are separate words before the noun; they replace the article and take the endings of ein (with a plural: meine). Two separate choices: the owner chooses sein (his, its) or ihr (her, their), the owned noun the ending: seine Frau (his wife), ihr Mann (her husband). An article is never added to a possessive before a noun.

examples.text: Anna und ihr Bruder – Max und seine Schwester

examples.note: euer drops its e before an ending

model.other: DET.poss (16 cells), 7 lexemes incl. de:Ihr.poss; inflect class poss; transform Number and Formality.

phenomena.title: No possessive endings on nouns
phenomena.what: Possession is never an ending on the possessed noun. A possessive determiner stands before the noun and replaces the article (mein Haus, unser Auto); a possessor noun follows in the genitive or with von + dative (das Haus meines Vaters, das Haus von meinem Vater). The possessed noun keeps its form.

examples.text: mein Haus – dein Haus – sein Haus
examples.note: my / your / his house: the noun never changes

model.other: Comparison notes (D18): fn.possessive notes (tr, fi, hu, fa, ar, he, iu).

phenomena.title: One kind of possession
phenomena.what: All possessed nouns are treated alike: body parts and relatives (meine Hand, meine Mutter) take the same possessives as things one owns (mein Auto). With body parts and clothes the possessor is, however, often a dative of the person plus the article: Ich wasche mir die Hände (I wash my hands), Er hat sich das Bein gebrochen (he broke his leg).

examples.note: the same possessive for a relative and a thing
body part: dative of the person + article

phenomena.gap: Say it in the overview for learners whose languages distinguish alienable and inalienable possession; the dative of the body part comes later.

phenomena.title: Personal pronouns in three cases
phenomena.what: Personal pronouns have their own accusative and dative forms: ich – mich – mir, du – dich – dir, er – ihn – ihm, sie – sie – ihr, wir – uns – uns, ihr – euch – euch, sie – sie – ihnen, Sie – Sie – Ihnen. The genitive forms (meiner, deiner) survive only in fixed phrases.

examples.text: Ich mag dich. – Ich helfe dir.

model.other: PRON paradigm with NOM/ACC/DAT; inflect PRON;ACC (fn.object), PRON;DAT (fn.case); wer has NOM/ACC/DAT/GEN (class intp).

phenomena.title: Demonstratives: dieser, der … da
phenomena.what: A demonstrative stands before the noun and replaces the article: dieser Mann, diese Frau, dieses Kind, diese Kinder, with the article's endings. Speech usually points with the stressed article and hier / da (der Mann da, das Buch hier); jener (that) is written and formal. Pointing at something without naming it uses das, which never changes: Das ist ein Tisch. Das sind Kinder.

examples.text: dieser Tisch – diese Lampe – dieses Bett

phenomena.title: er, sie, es follow the noun's gender, not the sex
phenomena.what: A pronoun copies the grammatical gender of its noun: der Tisch → er, die Lampe → sie, das Buch → es, every plural → sie. With das Mädchen the grammar asks for es, though people often switch to sie once they know her name.

examples.text: Wo ist der Schlüssel? – Er ist auf dem Tisch.

model.other: Taught in fn.pronoun.subject (callout “Things are er, sie or es”); profile senses of de:er, de:sie, de:es say ‘it’ for nouns of that gender.

phenomena.title: One ‘we’
phenomena.what: wir means ‘I and others’ whether or not the person spoken to is included: Wir gehen ins Kino may include the listener or not. Context or a phrase makes it clear (wir beide, wir zwei; wir ohne dich).

examples.note: with or without the listener – the same wir
let's go: here the listener is included

model.other: Comparison notes (D18): fn.pronoun.subject and fn.overview notes (mr: āpaṇ / āmhī).

phenomena.title: man – the impersonal ‘one, you, people’
phenomena.alsoNote: fr on, nl men, sv man are the same impersonal subject pronoun. en one / generic you partly.
phenomena.what: man is the everyday impersonal subject: ‘one, you, people, they’ (Man sagt … – people say …). It takes the er-form of the verb and has the object forms einen, einem; it is never replaced by er. Because a clause needs a subject, man fills the place where the doer is general or unknown.

examples.text: Wie sagt man das auf Deutsch?
examples.note: How do you say that in German?

phenomena.title: es as an empty subject; es gibt
phenomena.alsoNote: Dummy subjects with weather verbs and an existential: en it rains / there is, fr il pleut / il y a, nl het regent / er is, sv det regnar / det finns.
phenomena.what: Every finite clause needs a subject in the nominative that the verb agrees with, whatever stands in first place – even when nobody acts: es is an empty subject with weather verbs (es regnet), in fixed phrases (Wie geht es dir?) and in es gibt (there is). ‘There is / are’ is es gibt + accusative (Es gibt hier einen Park), not haben or sein.

examples.note: how are you? (literally: how goes it to you)

phenomena.record: A fixed construction (lexeme es_gibt or a frame), not a word property.
