phenomena.title: Reflexive verbs and pronouns: sich
phenomena.alsoNote: Reflexive pronoun with the verb and inherently reflexive verbs; cs se/si and bg се/си even split accusative and dative like mich/mir. ru, uk have reflexive verbs with the suffix -ся/-сь instead of a pronoun.
phenomena.what: Many verbs need a reflexive pronoun: mich, dich, sich, uns, euch, sich (accusative) or mir, dir, sich (dative when there is another object). Some verbs are only reflexive (sich freuen), others change meaning (verlassen → sich verlassen auf, to rely on).

examples.note: sich verlassen auf = to rely on (de:verlassen sense)

phenomena.record: features.reflexive: [{case: ACC | DAT, senses}] – the meanings that need the reflexive pronoun, or none.

model.other: Every verb states it; one reflexive meaning in the course: de:verlassen s3 (sich verlassen auf).

phenomena.gap: Reflexive pronoun forms (PRON cells with REFL) and the cr.07 lesson.

phenomena.title: The verb does not mark its object
phenomena.what: The verb agrees only with its subject. An object – noun or pronoun – is a separate word in the accusative or dative (Ich sehe ihn. Ich gebe ihr das Buch.); the verb form is the same whatever the object, definite or not, and object pronouns are never attached to the verb.

examples.text: Ich sehe den Hund. – Ich sehe einen Hund. – Ich sehe ihn.

model.other: Comparison notes (D18): fn.object notes (sw, lg, iu) and fn.present note (hu: definite conjugation).

phenomena.title: Relative pronouns der, die, das (dessen, denen)
phenomena.what: Relative clauses follow the noun they describe and start with a relative pronoun – der, die, das in the gender and number of the noun and the case of its role in the clause; the verb goes to the end. The forms are the article's, except dessen, deren (genitive) and denen (dative plural).

examples.text: die Frau, deren Sohn Arzt ist

model.other: Profile senses only (de:was ‘alles, was …’, de:wo ‘die Stadt, wo ich wohne’, de:welcher relative).

phenomena.gap: A relative-pronoun lexeme (PRON.rel paradigm) and the cr.06 lesson with `combine`.

phenomena.title: da- and wo- compounds: darauf, worauf
phenomena.alsoNote: Dutch daarop, waarmee, er … op are the same construction. en (thereby, whereupon) and sv (därpå, varmed) keep it in formal or old style only.
phenomena.what: A preposition with a pronoun for a thing becomes da(r)- + preposition (darauf, damit, dafür), in questions wo(r)- (worauf, womit). For persons the preposition + pronoun stays: auf ihn, auf wen.

examples.text: Ich warte auf den Bus. → Ich warte darauf.
Worauf wartest du? – Auf wen wartest du?

phenomena.record: Each da-/wo- form as a lexeme linked to its preposition.
phenomena.gap: Lexemes (or a derived table per preposition) and a lesson after the verbs with prepositional objects.

phenomena.title: Strong, weak and mixed adjective endings
phenomena.alsoNote: Strong/weak/mixed endings by the preceding determiner combined with case are German. Partly: sv, nl (strong/weak split without case: en stor bil / den stora bilen, een groot huis / het grote huis); sr, lt (definite and indefinite adjective forms); ru, el, pl (gender-number-case agreement without determiner dependence).
phenomena.what: An adjective before its noun always has an ending, chosen by the word in front of it: after der/dieser (weak) only -e or -en; after ein/kein/mein without an ending (mixed) the adjective shows the gender itself (-er, -es); with no article (strong) it takes the article's ending. In the dative the ending after any article is -en. A few adjectives change their stem when they take an ending: ein hohes Haus, ein dunkles Bier, ein teures Auto.

examples.text: der große Tisch – ein großer Tisch – großer Hunger
mit dem neuen Auto, in einer kleinen Wohnung
zwei kleine Kinder – die kleinen Kinder

phenomena.record: features.adjAfter on determiners (weak | mixed | strong) and features.stem on adjectives (hoh-, dunkl-, teur-, or none).

model.other: Every determiner states the adjective declension it triggers (der, dieser, jener, alle, manche, welcher → weak; ein, kein, the possessives → mixed; viel, wenig, einige, ein bisschen, wie viel(e) → strong); every adjective its stem before an ending. language.json ADJ paradigm: 12 cells × STRG/WEAK/MIX; fn.adjective inflect generators.

phenomena.gap: No genitive adjective cells; the app does not yet generate or check article + adjective + noun phrases from adjAfter.

phenomena.title: Predicative and adverbial adjectives do not change
phenomena.alsoNote: Dutch predicative adjectives have no ending and the adverb is the bare adjective (het huis is groot, hij rijdt snel). en: predicative invariable but adverbs mostly in -ly; fr, es, it, el, ru: the predicative adjective agrees.
phenomena.what: An adjective used as the predicate needs the verb sein (or werden, bleiben) and has no ending there: Das Haus ist groß, Die Häuser sind groß. The same bare form is the adverb, with no adverb suffix: Er fährt schnell.

model.other: ADJ citation cell ‘ADJ’; fn.agreement callout “After sein: no ending”.

phenomena.title: Comparison: -er, am -sten, umlaut, irregulars
phenomena.what: The comparative adds -er (+ als), the superlative is am …-sten (predicate, adverb) or der …-ste (before a noun). Short adjectives often add umlaut; a few are irregular. Equality is so … wie.

examples.text: gut – besser – am besten; viel – mehr – am meisten; hoch – höher – am höchsten
Der Zug ist schneller als der Bus.

phenomena.record: features.comparison (ADJ: regular | umlaut | irregular | not compared; ADV: [comparative, superlative] or none); the ADJ forms in ADJ;CMPR, ADJ;SPRL.

model.other: ADJ;CMPR, ADJ;SPRL and four weak superlative cells; fn.comparison generators (inflect, bank).

phenomena.title: Adjectives without endings: rosa, lila, orange, Berliner
phenomena.what: A few colour words borrowed from other languages (rosa, lila, orange, beige) take no endings in careful German (ein rosa Kleid); speech often adds them. Adjectives from place names in -er never change (der Berliner Bahnhof, Neuseeländer Spinat).

model.other: class inv on de:rosa, de:lila, de:orange (paradigm ADJ.inv = one cell); fn.comparison trap.

phenomena.title: Present tense: endings, stem-vowel change, no progressive
phenomena.what: The present adds -e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en to the stem, one ending for each person and number; polite Sie takes the plural form. The simple present covers ongoing, habitual and – with a time word – future events: Ich koche = I cook / I am cooking. An ongoing action can be stressed with gerade or, colloquially, am + infinitive (Ich bin am Kochen), but this is never required. Many strong verbs change the stem vowel in the du and er forms only: essen → isst, fahren → fährt, laufen → läuft (the imperative keeps i but drops the umlaut: Iss! Fahr!).

examples.text: ich kaufe, du kaufst, er kauft, wir kaufen, ihr kauft, sie kaufen

phenomena.record: features.presentChange: no change | e>i | e>ie | a>ä | au>äu | irregular.

model.other: VERB paradigm cells (all required); inflect over all known verbs (separable ones excluded). fn.present callout “No -ing form”. Forms stored; inflect generators for essen/mögen/wollen (fn.present) and fahren/laufen/verlassen (fn.direction); imperative traps.

phenomena.title: No grammatical aspect
phenomena.what: Verbs have no perfective / imperfective pairs and no aspect markers: one verb form serves a completed or an ongoing action (Ich las das Buch – I read / was reading the book). Completion, duration and repetition are added when needed by adverbs (gerade, schon, fertig, immer wieder), by particle verbs (essen – aufessen, eat up) or by context. The choice between perfect and Präteritum is a matter of register, not of aspect.

examples.note: finished or in progress – the same form

model.other: fn.past says that the Perfekt / Präteritum choice is register, not aspect; fn.past.ongoing (status periphrastic) shows habits and backgrounds with früher, immer, oft, als / während and the colloquial am-progressive; comparison notes for el, ru, es, fr, hi, tr, ko, fi … (aspect pairs, imperfect, progressive forms).

phenomena.title: Weak, strong and mixed verbs; principal parts
phenomena.alsoNote: The Germanic strong (ablaut) / weak (dental suffix) verb classes: en sing – sang – sung / walk – walked, nl, sv likewise. Principal parts to learn are familiar from el, la, Romance irregular verbs, without the ablaut classes.
phenomena.what: Weak verbs form the past with -te and the participle ge-…-t (kaufen – kaufte – gekauft). Strong verbs change the stem vowel (ablaut) and form the participle in -en (trinken – trank – getrunken). Mixed verbs change the vowel and take weak endings (rennen – rannte – gerannt). Inseparable prefixes and -ieren verbs have no ge- (verlassen, studiert). The principal parts are learned with each strong verb (singen – sang – gesungen).

examples.text: trinken – trank – getrunken; gehen – ging – gegangen

examples.note: no ge- after an inseparable prefix

phenomena.record: features.principalParts (infinitive, 3 SG present, 3 SG Präteritum, Partizip II) and features.conjugation: weak | strong | mixed | modal | irregular.

model.other: All verbs state their four principal parts and their class; the 22 verbs of cr.01–cr.03 store the whole Präteritum. fn.past drills the Partizip II (inflect V;PTCP;PST, separable verbs listed by lemma), fn.past.ongoing the Präteritum rows.

phenomena.gap: The word card does not show the Präteritum and the Partizip II from principalParts yet (langcore shows the du / er forms and the auxiliary); no ablaut-series exercise; V;PST;* and V;PTCP;PST are not required cells in language.json, and the foundation verbs store only V;PST;3;SG.

phenomena.title: Modal verbs
phenomena.what: können, müssen, dürfen, sollen, wollen, mögen (and möchte) have no ending in ich and er and a different vowel in the singular (ich kann, er muss); the second verb goes to the end in the infinitive without zu.

examples.text: ich will – er will; ich mag – er mag
ich kann, er muss, du darfst

model.other: conjugation “modal” on de:wollen and de:mögen (with möchte cells V;SBJV;PST and senseForms); fn.present table and flow block.

phenomena.gap: können, müssen, dürfen, sollen (cr.04); lassen and the bare infinitive after gehen / bleiben are not marked.

phenomena.title: Separable verbs
phenomena.what: A stressed particle (an, ab, auf, aus, ein, mit, weg, zurück, her-, hin- …) belongs to the verb but goes to the end of a main clause; in a subordinate clause and in the infinitive it is joined again; ge- and zu go between particle and stem (angekommen, anzukommen). The particle often changes the meaning unpredictably: ankommen (arrive) – es kommt darauf an (it depends).

examples.text: ankommen: Der Zug kommt um acht an.
…, weil der Zug um acht ankommt.
Der Zug kommt an. – Es kommt darauf an.

phenomena.record: features.separable: the particle, or none.

model.other: 14 verbs with `separable` and a V;SEP cell (aufwachen, aufstehen, anziehen, losgehen, anfangen, aufhören, heimkommen, einschlafen, aufwachsen added in cr.01–cr.02); fn.past teaches ge- inside the participle (aufgestanden); inflect skips separable verbs unless listed, because one cell holds only the stem form. A separable verb in a subordinate clause (… als er heimkam) cannot be written yet: there is no joined finite form.

phenomena.gap: No zu-infinitive cell and no joined finite form for subordinate clauses (heimkam, ankommt); no drill of the whole form (kommt … an) and of the particle position; particle verbs listed in profiles are not lexemes.

phenomena.title: Inseparable prefixes – and prefixes that can be both
phenomena.alsoNote: Dutch be-, ver-, ont-, ge-, her- are unstressed, never separate and block ge- (vergeten); door-, over-, om-, onder- can be both. ru, pl, cs and other fixed-prefix languages know prefixes that stay on the verb and change its meaning.
phenomena.what: These prefixes never separate, are never stressed and block ge- in the participle. They often change the meaning or make a verb transitive: verlassen (leave a place, + accusative) vs weggehen. durch-, über-, um-, unter- can be either: übersetzen (translate, inseparable) – übersetzen (ferry across, separable).

examples.text: verlassen – Ich verlasse das Haus. – Ich habe das Haus verlassen.
Er fährt den Baum um. – Er umfährt den Stau.

phenomena.record: features.inseparable: be | emp | ent | er | ge | miss | ver | zer, or none.

model.other: Inseparable prefixes: verlassen (ver-), beginnen, beenden, besuchen (be-), erinnern (er-), vergessen (ver-); fn.past teaches “no ge-” (begonnen, beendet, vergessen) together with -ieren (reserviert).

phenomena.gap: No drill that contrasts separable and inseparable verbs, and no stress information (no ipa).

phenomena.title: The object noun stays outside the verb
phenomena.what: A noun object is a phrase of its own with its article and case; it is not built into the verb, and verb + object does not form a fixed compound that splits in some forms. A few verbs were made from a noun and a verb (staubsaugen, frühstücken) but behave as ordinary verbs; in set phrases like Rad fahren and Klavier spielen the noun is written apart and stands where an object stands (Ich fahre gern Rad).

examples.note: the object is a separate phrase with an article
a set phrase: the bare noun stays a separate word

model.other: Comparison notes (D18): fn.overview note (iu); fn.object notes (iu; zh for verb–object compounds such as 吃饭).

phenomena.title: Perfect with haben or sein
phenomena.alsoNote: Choice between ‘have’ and ‘be’ in the perfect: fr avoir/être, it avere/essere, nl hebben/zijn. en, es, sv, el, sq use ‘have’ only.
phenomena.what: The perfect is formed with an auxiliary + the Partizip II at the end of the clause: haben (‘have’) for most verbs, sein for verbs of motion or change of state without an object (gehen, fahren, kommen, bleiben, sein). A verb can take both: Ich bin nach Berlin gefahren / Ich habe das Auto gefahren. South German and Austrian use sein also with stehen, sitzen, liegen.

examples.text: Ich bin nach Hause gegangen. Ich bin hier geblieben.
Ich bin nach Berlin gefahren. – Ich habe das Auto gefahren.
examples.note: fahren: sein without object, haben with one

phenomena.record: features.aux: haben | sein | both, and features.auxBySense: [{aux, senses, when?}] for the verbs whose auxiliary depends on the meaning or on a direct object.

model.other: All 45 verbs state aux; fn.past (cr.01) teaches haben / sein (callout and quiz), with sein for aufstehen, aufwachen, einschlafen, losgehen, heimkommen, aufwachsen and haben for reflexive verbs (Ich habe mich angezogen).

phenomena.gap: South German / Austrian sein with stehen, sitzen, liegen is not recorded (those verbs are not course words).

phenomena.title: Perfekt in speech, Präteritum in writing
phenomena.alsoNote: French has the same split: passé composé in speech, passé simple in written narrative. Partly: ro (perfect simplu mainly literary/regional), it (passato remoto rare in northern speech).
phenomena.what: German has one past tense, without degrees of remoteness, in two forms. Spoken German tells the past mostly with the perfect (Ich habe gegessen), written narrative with the Präteritum (Er aß). sein, haben and the modals use the Präteritum in speech too (war, hatte, wollte). The south uses the perfect almost only; the north uses more Präteritum. A finite verb always shows present or past.

model.other: fn.past (cr.01) teaches the Perfekt and the register split (Perfekt in speech, Präteritum in writing; war / hatte in speech); fn.past.ongoing (cr.02) the Präteritum of weak and strong verbs. The 22 verbs of cr.01–cr.03 store the full Präteritum (6 cells) and the Partizip II; Tense transforms (present → Perfekt / Präteritum) in lang/de/bank/c01_04.json.

phenomena.gap: sein, haben, the modals and the other verbs of the foundations store only V;PST;3;SG (their lexicon files predate cr.01), so the bank can use war / hatte only with er / sie / es; their full Präteritum rows are needed.

phenomena.title: The future: present + time word, or werden
phenomena.what: With a time word the present already means the future (Morgen komme ich zurück). werden + infinitive marks the future or a guess (Er wird schon zu Hause sein). werden alone means ‘to become’ (Ich werde Lehrerin).

model.other: de:werden (cr.03: the future auxiliary, role; its meaning “to become” is the pending concept verb.become); fn.future (status periphrastic): present + time word (nächste Woche, nächstes Jahr, morgen) and werden + infinitive, Tense transforms present → Futur I.

phenomena.title: Konjunktiv II: politeness and unreal conditions
phenomena.what: Konjunktiv II makes polite requests (möchte, hätte gern, könnten Sie) and unreal conditions (Wenn ich Zeit hätte, würde ich kommen). Most verbs use würde + infinitive; sein, haben, modals and a few strong verbs use their own forms (wäre, hätte, könnte).

examples.text: Wenn ich Zeit hätte, würde ich kommen.

model.other: V;SBJV;PST cells only for de:mögen (möchte); 8 bank tokens.

phenomena.gap: Konjunktiv II of sein, haben, modals and würde; cr.05.

phenomena.title: No optative mood
phenomena.what: No verb form serves only for wishes. Wishes use Konjunktiv II with doch or nur (Wenn ich doch Zeit hätte! Hätte ich nur …), a verb or adverb of wishing (Ich wünsche dir …, Hoffentlich …), or fixed old Konjunktiv I formulas (Es lebe die Freiheit! Gott sei Dank).

examples.note: if only I had time: Konjunktiv II + doch
I hope she comes: an adverb

phenomena.gap: Wishes come with Konjunktiv II (cr.05); say there that German has no separate wish form.

phenomena.title: Konjunktiv I: reported speech
phenomena.what: Konjunktiv I marks what someone else said, so the speaker does not vouch for it: er sei, er habe, er komme (newspapers, formal reports). The modal sollen does the same for hearsay (Er soll sehr reich sein – he is said to be very rich), wollen for a claim about oneself (Er will nichts gesehen haben – he claims he saw nothing). In speech the indicative or Konjunktiv II replaces Konjunktiv I.

examples.text: Sie sagte, sie habe keine Zeit.
examples.note: she said she had no time

phenomena.gap: Konjunktiv I cells (at least 3 SG) and a reading-level lesson.

phenomena.title: No grammatical mirativity
phenomena.what: Surprise or unexpected new information is not marked in the verb. It is expressed by intonation, by modal particles (Das ist ja toll! Du bist aber groß geworden!) and by words such as wirklich, tatsächlich, na so was.
phenomena.gap: Say it with the modal particles for learners whose languages mark surprise in the verb.

phenomena.title: Two passives: werden and sein
phenomena.alsoNote: Two passives, of the action and of the resulting state: nl worden/zijn, es and pt ser/estar, pl zostać/być + participle. Partly: it venire/essere, en be/get.
phenomena.what: werden + participle describes an action being done (Vorgangspassiv), sein + participle the resulting state (Zustandspassiv). The doer is von + dative.

examples.text: Das Buch wurde von Goethe geschrieben.

phenomena.gap: werden lexeme and a passive lesson with `transform` (active ↔ passive).

phenomena.title: No antipassive
phenomena.what: A transitive verb can simply be used without its object (Ich esse. Er liest gern.), with no special verb form; the subject stays in the nominative. An unspecified object is left out or said with etwas (Er liest etwas).

examples.note: I am eating: the object left out, the verb unchanged

model.other: Comparison notes (D18): fn.overview note (iu).

phenomena.title: No causative verb form
phenomena.what: Making or letting someone do something is said with the separate verb lassen + infinitive (Ich lasse das Auto reparieren – I have the car repaired; Sie lässt ihn schlafen – she lets him sleep) or with machen (Das macht mich müde). A few old verb pairs are causative in meaning but are separate words learned one by one: setzen – sitzen, legen – liegen, stellen – stehen, fällen – fallen.

examples.text: Ich lege das Buch auf den Tisch. – Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch.
examples.note: a lexical pair, not a regular form

phenomena.gap: lassen is not in the course yet; a later lesson on lassen + infinitive.

phenomena.title: No applicative
phenomena.what: The verb has no form that turns a beneficiary, place or instrument into its object. Such participants are datives or prepositional phrases (Ich koche dir eine Suppe. Ich koche für dich.). The prefix be- can make a place the object (Er klebt Plakate an die Wand → Er beklebt die Wand mit Plakaten), but it makes new verbs one by one, not a regular form of every verb.

examples.text: Er beklebt die Wand mit Plakaten.
examples.note: be-: a derived verb with the place as object

model.other: Comparison notes (D18): fn.overview note (sw).

phenomena.gap: Said for Swahili in the overview; be- verbs (beschenken …) come with derivation (later).

phenomena.title: Three imperatives: du, ihr, Sie
phenomena.what: One person you say du to: the stem (Komm! Geh! Warte!); several: the ihr form (Kommt!); anyone you say Sie to: infinitive + Sie (Kommen Sie!). Let's = wir form with the verb first (Gehen wir!).

model.other: IMP cells for 18 verbs (not heißen, haben, mögen, wollen, kochen); formsAlt holds Gehe!/Komme!; transform Mood and Formality (8 + bank).

phenomena.title: Infinitive with and without zu
phenomena.alsoNote: An infinitive marker with bare infinitives after modals: en to / can go, nl te / kan gaan, sv att / kan gå. Partly: fr, it, es (prepositions de/à, di/a before an infinitive); ru, el have no infinitive marker.
phenomena.what: Most verbs, nouns and adjectives take zu + infinitive at the end of the clause (Ich habe keine Zeit zu kochen); um … zu means ‘in order to’. Modals (and lassen, gehen, sehen, hören) take the bare infinitive. With a separable verb zu goes inside: anzukommen.

examples.text: Ich habe keine Zeit zu kochen.
Ich gehe in die Stadt, um Brot zu kaufen.

model.other: Profile sense of de:zu; modal + bare infinitive in fn.present.

phenomena.gap: A zu-infinitive cell for separable verbs and a lesson (cr.04 / later).

phenomena.title: Clauses joined by conjunctions: no serial verbs, converbs or switch reference
phenomena.what: Two actions in sequence are two finite verbs joined by und (Ich gehe nach Hause und koche), an infinitive with zu or um … zu, or a subordinate clause with a conjunction (Nachdem ich gegessen hatte, …). Verbs are not strung together without a link, no special non-finite form chains clauses (a present participle such as lachend is rare and literary), and the verb never shows whether the next clause has the same subject – pronouns do. Only a few verbs take a bare infinitive of a second verb: gehen, kommen, bleiben, lassen (Ich gehe schwimmen).

examples.text: Ich gehe nach Hause und koche.
examples.note: two finite verbs joined by und

examples.text: Nachdem ich gegessen hatte, ging ich.
examples.note: a conjunction, not a verb form, links the clauses

model.other: Comparison notes (D18): fn.connectors notes (tr, ja, ko, iu).

phenomena.gap: Converbs and verb-ending clause links are said in the fn.connectors notes; serial verbs (zh, vi, yo …) are not said yet – careful: gehen + infinitive (Ich gehe einkaufen) exists.

phenomena.title: Verb second in statements, verb first in yes/no questions and commands
phenomena.what: In a statement the conjugated verb is always the second element. Anything can come first – the subject, a time word, an object, a whole subordinate clause – and then the subject follows the verb. So subject and object have no fixed order (Der Hund sieht den Mann. – Den Mann sieht der Hund.): the case, not the position, tells them apart. A yes/no question and a command put the verb first, with no auxiliary added (Trinkst du Tee? Kommen Sie herein!).

examples.text: Ich trinke heute Tee. – Heute trinke ich Tee. – Tee trinke ich heute.
examples.note: the verb stays in place two

examples.text: Am Montag gehe ich zur Arbeit.
Weil es kalt ist, trinken wir Tee.
examples.note: a clause in first place, then the verb
the second verb stays at the end

model.other: Bank sentences carry `alts` for other correct orders; build_sentence checks the order against text + alts; fn.present callout “Verb second”. transform Mood INT (42 bank variants) and IMP (8); word_order on yes/no questions.

phenomena.title: No question particle
phenomena.what: A yes/no question is made by moving the conjugated verb to the front (Trinkst du Tee?) or, in speech, by a rising intonation alone (Du trinkst Tee?); no particle marks a question. A tag can be added at the end to ask for agreement (…, oder? …, nicht? …, ne?), but it is optional.

model.other: Comparison notes (D18): fn.question.yesno notes (tr, ja, zh, mr, hi, fa, fi …).

phenomena.title: Question words come first
phenomena.what: In a question-word question the question word, or the phrase with it, goes to the start, the conjugated verb follows in second place, then the subject: Was trinkst du? Mit wem sprichst du? Welches Buch liest du? All question words start with w- (was, wer, wo, wann, wie, warum, welcher); wer declines (wen, wem, wessen). A question word left in place (Du hast was gemacht?) makes only an echo question of surprise.

examples.note: the whole phrase moves to the front

phenomena.title: Verb at the end of subordinate clauses
phenomena.what: Subordinate clauses are finite clauses introduced by a conjunction (weil, dass, wenn, als, ob, obwohl), a question word (indirect questions) or a relative pronoun, and in all of them the conjugated verb goes to the end; a separable verb joins its particle there, a modal comes last. Spoken German often keeps main-clause order after weil (weil ich habe Durst) – common, but wrong in writing.

examples.text: …, weil der Zug um acht ankommt.
Ich weiß nicht, wann er kommt.

model.other: fn.connectors (40 bank sentences) with the three connector groups and the spoken-weil callout.

phenomena.title: The sentence bracket (Satzklammer)
phenomena.what: The finite verb in second place and the rest of the verb at the end frame the sentence: a modal + infinitive, a separable verb + particle, the perfect auxiliary + participle, werden + infinitive. Everything else stands inside the bracket, however long.

examples.text: Ich will heute Abend Tee trinken.
Der Zug kommt um acht Uhr an.

model.other: Modal brackets (fd.07), separable brackets (fd.13), perfect brackets (auxiliary … participle, cr.01) and future brackets (werden … infinitive, cr.03) appear in the bank; no exercise asks for the slot of the second verb part.

phenomena.gap: A `word_order` generator that removes the bracket’s second part and asks where it goes; passive brackets come later.

phenomena.title: Order inside the sentence: time – manner – place; pronouns first
phenomena.what: Between the verb and the end, time usually comes before manner and place (‘te-ka-mo-lo’), pronouns come before nouns, a dative noun before an accusative noun but an accusative pronoun before a dative pronoun, and nicht stands before what it negates or at the end.

examples.text: Ich fahre morgen mit dem Bus nach Berlin.
Ich gebe dem Kind das Buch. – Ich gebe es ihm.
examples.note: nouns: dative first; pronouns: accusative first

examples.text: Ich esse den Fisch nicht. – Das ist nicht gut.
examples.note: nicht at the end / before the adjective

model.other: fn.time.day (“time comes before manner and place”); fn.negation (position of nicht).

phenomena.gap: Object order (dative/accusative, pronouns) comes only with cr.03; no exercise targets the order of the middle field.

phenomena.title: nicht or kein – and only one negation
phenomena.what: kein (a negative article, declined like ein, with a plural) negates a noun that would have ein or no article; nicht, a separate word, negates everything else – verbs, adjectives, places, and nouns with der, dieser or a possessive. nicht stands before the part it negates or, for the whole clause, near the end. Only one negative word per clause: Ich esse nichts, Ich habe niemanden gesehen – a second negation is not added.

examples.text: Ich habe kein Brot. – Ich trinke keinen Kaffee.

model.other: de:kein (class neg, 16 cells), de:nicht; transform Polarity (49 bank variants). fn.negation callout “Only one negation”; lexemes de:nichts, de:niemand, de:nie, de:niemals, de:weder, de:noch.

phenomena.title: doch – ‘yes’ against a negative
phenomena.alsoNote: A special ‘yes’ against a negative: sv jo, nl jawel, fr si, ar بلى balā. en has none.
phenomena.what: To contradict a negative question or statement, German answers doch, not ja: Isst du kein Fleisch? – Doch! (Yes, I do). nein confirms the negative (Nein, ich esse keins). ja answers a positive question.

examples.text: Du kommst nicht mit? – Doch, ich komme mit.

model.other: de:doch (PART, role); fn.question.yesno callout.

phenomena.title: Prepositions fix the case
phenomena.what: German uses prepositions (only a few postpositions: meiner Meinung nach, den Fluss entlang). Each preposition takes a fixed case: aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu + dative; bis, durch, für, gegen, ohne, um + accusative; während, wegen, trotz + genitive (spoken often dative): mit meinem Bruder, für meinen Bruder.

examples.text: für meinen Vater, ohne meinen Bruder

phenomena.record: features.governs: [{case, senses?, when?}] – the case of each meaning of the preposition (two-way: DAT for where?, ACC for where to?); a contraction states the case of its article.

model.other: Every ADP states the case per meaning: über ACC for “about” (s1), DAT for “above” (s2), ACC for “across / via”; in and an DAT for the time senses (im Mai, am Montag); während GEN (everyday DAT noted); meanings that are not prepositional (zu “too”, auf “open”) are in no item.

phenomena.title: Two-way prepositions: Wo? dative, Wohin? accusative
phenomena.alsoNote: Location vs goal with the same preposition and two cases: ru в/на + prepositional vs accusative, pl, cs, sr, uk likewise, la in + ablative vs accusative.
phenomena.what: in, an, auf, über, unter, vor, hinter, neben, zwischen take the dative for a place (Wo?) and the accusative for a goal (Wohin?): Ich bin im Park – Ich gehe in den Park.

examples.text: Ich bin im Park. – Ich gehe in den Park.
Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch. – Ich lege das Buch auf den Tisch.

model.other: governs per meaning on 9 two-way prepositions (DAT for where?, ACC for where to?, and the one-case meanings: über “about” + ACC, an / in for time + DAT); fn.prep.place and fn.direction with bank sentences.

phenomena.gap: The `contrast` exercise (Akk vs Dat with the reason) is not implemented.

phenomena.title: Verbs that govern a case or a preposition
phenomena.what: Most verbs take an accusative object, but some take the dative (helfen, danken, gehören, gefallen, antworten) or a fixed preposition with a fixed case (warten auf + accusative, denken an + accusative, sich freuen über / auf). These have to be learned with the verb.
phenomena.record: features.governs: [{case, prep?, senses, note?}] – the object cases, prepositional objects and predicative nominatives of each meaning, or none.

model.other: Every verb states its frame per meaning: kaufen ACC (+ DAT), warten auf + ACC (s1) / ACC (s2 maintain), ankommen auf + ACC (s2) / bei + DAT (s3), gehen DAT (s4 es geht mir gut), heißen NOM (predicative).

phenomena.gap: Dative verbs (helfen, gefallen) come in cr.03; no drill ‘which case after this verb’.

phenomena.title: Body states: Mir ist kalt, Ich habe Hunger
phenomena.alsoNote: Person in the dative for body states and liking: ru мне холодно, мне нравится; pl zimno mi; cs je mi zima; sr hladno mi je. fr, es, it, pt share only ‘have hunger/cold’ (j'ai faim, tengo hambre).
phenomena.what: Feelings of the body and impersonal states take the person in the dative: Mir ist kalt (I'm cold – Ich bin kalt means ‘I am a cold person’), Mir ist schlecht (I feel sick), Wie geht es dir?, Das gefällt mir. Hunger and thirst use haben + a bare noun: Ich habe Hunger, Ich habe Durst (also Angst, Zeit, Recht haben).

examples.note: I'm hungry (hungrig sein is more formal)

model.other: fn.adjective and fn.copula traps; the greeting lexemes with dir / Ihnen. de:Hunger, de:Durst (NOUN, senses [], role) beside de:hungrig, de:durstig; fn.have callout.

phenomena.gap: Bank sentences with Mir ist kalt/warm/schlecht and a transform (person change); gefallen in cr.03. Angst, Recht, Glück, Zeit are not lexemes; the collocation is not a stored unit.

phenomena.title: Preposition + article in one word: im, zum, zur …
phenomena.alsoNote: Obligatory preposition + article contractions: fr au/du, it nel/al/del, pt no/do/ao, es al/del, el στο/στη/στον. Partly: ga (sa + an = san). en and nl (apart from old ter/ten) have none.
phenomena.what: Some prepositions merge with dem, der or das: im, am, beim, vom, zum (dem), zur (der), ins, ans (das). The merged form is the normal one; in dem Park sounds like ‘in that park’. Speech also says aufm, unterm, hinterm.

examples.text: in dem → im Park; zu der → zur Schule

phenomena.record: features.contractions: [{form, article, lexeme?, register?}] on the preposition, or none; the contractions themselves are lexemes with role.

model.other: Every preposition lists its merged forms (in → im, ins; zu → zum, zur; auf → aufs; für → fürs; um → ums; colloquial: übers, überm, unterm, unters, vorm, vors, hinterm, hinters); the 8 merged forms of the course (de:im … de:vom) are lexemes with role and are linked from their preposition.

phenomena.title: Where German uses an article and where not
phenomena.alsoNote: Article rules are language-particular. nl is closest (no article with jobs after zijn, mass nouns bare, most countries bare) but differs for months and some countries; fr omits the article with jobs but uses it with countries and the partitive with masses.
phenomena.what: No article with a job, role or nationality after sein (Ich bin Lehrerin), with mass nouns in general (Ich trinke Wasser) and with most country names (nach Griechenland). An article with feminine and plural country names (in die Türkei, in der Schweiz, in den USA), with months and seasons (im Mai) and, in colloquial southern German, with first names (der Peter).

model.other: Callouts in fn.copula (no article with jobs), fn.object (food and drink), fn.direction (in die Türkei); profile sense of de:der (der Peter).

phenomena.gap: Country names are not course words; no exercise contrasts ‘article / no article’.

phenomena.title: Das ist / Das sind / Das bin ich
phenomena.alsoNote: Dutch Dat zijn mijn ouders, Dat ben ik – the verb agrees with what follows. fr ce sont partly (but c'est moi).
phenomena.what: In pointing sentences with das, the verb agrees with the noun or pronoun that follows, not with das: Das sind meine Eltern. Das bin ich.

examples.text: Das ist ein Kind. – Das sind Kinder.
Das bin ich. – Das sind wir.

model.other: fn.copula callout; transform Number.

phenomena.title: One verb sein for identity, quality and place
phenomena.what: sein links a subject to a noun (Ich bin Lehrerin), an adjective (Ich bin müde) and a place (Ich bin in Berlin) alike; there is no second verb ‘to be’ for location or for temporary states. The position of things is, however, often said with a posture verb (Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch), and existence with es gibt.

examples.text: Ich bin Lehrerin. – Ich bin müde. – Ich bin in Berlin.
examples.note: one verb sein for all three

model.other: Comparison notes (D18): fn.copula and fn.overview notes (es: ser / estar).

phenomena.title: haben: possession with a verb ‘have’
phenomena.what: Possession is said with the transitive verb haben: the owner is the subject in the nominative and the thing owned the object in the accusative (Ich habe einen Bruder. Hast du ein Auto?). haben also forms the perfect (Ich habe gegessen) and states such as Ich habe Hunger. Existence is es gibt + accusative, not haben.

phenomena.title: Long attributes before the noun
phenomena.alsoNote: A participle with its own complements before the noun: nl de om acht uur aankomende trein (formal), ru прибывающий в восемь поезд, fi kahdeksalta saapuva juna, hu a nyolckor érkező vonat, tr saat sekizde gelen tren (in fi, hu, tr the ordinary relative construction). en has no such construction; ja, ko put whole clauses before the noun.
phenomena.what: A participle with its own objects and adverbs can stand between the article and the noun: der um acht Uhr ankommende Zug (the train arriving at eight). It is frequent in written German; speech uses a relative clause after the noun instead (der Zug, der um acht Uhr ankommt).

examples.text: der um acht Uhr ankommende Zug

phenomena.gap: Present participle cells (V;PTCP;PRS) and a reading-level lesson.

phenomena.title: seit + present for something still going on
phenomena.alsoNote: A state still going on is said in the present with ‘since/for’: fr depuis, es desde hace, it da, ru уже … / с …, tr -dır, hu óta, ar منذ. en and sv use the perfect.
phenomena.what: Something that started in the past and still goes on is said in the present with seit, not in the perfect: Ich wohne seit drei Jahren hier (I have lived here for three years).

examples.text: Ich wohne seit drei Jahren hier.
examples.note: I have lived here for three years
We have been waiting for twenty minutes

model.other: fn.prep.time callout “seit + present”; de:seit governs DAT.

phenomena.title: Habit adverbs in -s: montags, morgens, abends
phenomena.alsoNote: Dutch 's maandags, 's avonds are the same old genitive adverbs. en Mondays / nights (I work nights) partly.
phenomena.what: A day or part of the day + -s, written small, means ‘every …, on …s’: montags (on Mondays), morgens, abends, nachts. With a clock time morgens/abends act as a.m./p.m.

examples.note: this morning (one time) – in the mornings (habit)

model.other: de:morgens, de:abends (ADV with role); fn.time.day.

phenomena.title: gehen, fahren, fliegen: the verb shows how you move
phenomena.what: The verb of movement says how one moves, and the direction goes into a particle, a prefix or a prepositional phrase: gehen on foot, fahren by any vehicle (also as a passenger), fliegen by plane; hineinlaufen (run in), über die Straße gehen (cross the street). Ich gehe nach Berlin sounds like walking there.

examples.text: Ich fahre mit dem Bus zur Schule.

phenomena.record: features.motion: on foot | by vehicle | by air | any means, or none (not a verb of motion).

model.other: de:gehen (verb.go), de:fahren (verb.drive, senses ‘go by vehicle’), de:laufen, de:rennen; fn.direction callout “gehen is not fahren”.

phenomena.gap: fliegen is not a course word (no verb.fly concept); the `sense_split` exercise (sort contexts into gehen / fahren / fliegen) is not implemented; the manner is stated per word, not per meaning.

phenomena.title: stellen / legen / setzen / hängen – stehen / liegen / sitzen / hängen
phenomena.what: Putting something somewhere and its being there are said with pairs that encode the position: upright (stellen → stehen), lying (legen → liegen), sitting (setzen → sitzen), hanging (hängen → hängen). The causing verb is weak and takes the accusative with two-way prepositions; the state verb is strong and takes the dative. Where a thing is, is normally said with the posture verb rather than sein: Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch, Die Flasche steht im Kühlschrank.

examples.text: Ich lege das Buch auf den Tisch. – Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch.
Ich stelle die Flasche in den Kühlschrank. – Die Flasche steht im Kühlschrank.
Ich setze das Kind auf den Stuhl. – Das Kind sitzt auf dem Stuhl.
Das Bild hängt an der Wand.

phenomena.record: Pairs linked (causative ↔ state) with position (upright / lying / sitting / hanging).

model.other: fn.prep.place uses ‘Ich lege das Buch auf den Tisch’ in its summary only; none of the verbs is a lexeme.

phenomena.gap: Concepts verb.put / be.located with the 8 lexemes, a `pair` link, and the `sense_split` / `contrast` exercises; the natural place is fd.12 (with the dative of place).

phenomena.title: kennen, wissen, können – verbs of knowing
phenomena.what: kennen is to be acquainted with a person, place or thing (Ich kenne Anna); wissen is to know a fact (Ich weiß, wo sie wohnt), with a clause or das/es/alles; können is to know how to do something or a language (Ich kann Deutsch).
phenomena.gap: A concept verb.know with the three lexemes (wissen has an irregular present: ich weiß, du weißt, er weiß) and a `sense_split` exercise.

phenomena.title: General verbs: tragen, schneiden
phenomena.what: Some everyday actions have one general verb whatever the object or the manner. tragen means both to wear (clothes, glasses, a ring, a hat: Sie trägt eine Brille) and to carry (Er trägt den Koffer); putting something on is anziehen, or aufsetzen for a hat or glasses. schneiden cuts anything with any blade (Brot, Haare, Papier); the manner is added only when needed (abschneiden, zerschneiden; sägen for a saw).

examples.note: he carries the suitcase – the same verb

phenomena.gap: tragen, anziehen and schneiden are not in the course lexicon yet (a clothes or kitchen field).

phenomena.title: Colour words
phenomena.what: The basic colour words are schwarz, weiß, rot, grün, blau, gelb, braun and grau, with rosa, lila and orange (which take no endings in careful German). Green and blue are always two separate words. Shades are made by compounds: hellblau, dunkelgrün, himmelblau, grasgrün.

examples.note: green and blue: two basic words

phenomena.title: hin and her: away from me, towards me
phenomena.alsoNote: Hungarian ide- (towards the speaker) / oda- (away) are deictic verb prefixes (idejön / odamegy), with hova/honnan questions. Partly: nl heen/naartoe; ru куда/откуда (question split only).
phenomena.what: Directional words mark the speaker's point of view: her- means towards the speaker, hin- away from the speaker (herein / hinein, herauf / hinauf). Spoken German shortens both to r- (rein, rauf). The question words split the same way: Wo gehst du hin? = Wohin gehst du?

examples.text: Wo kommst du her? = Woher kommst du?

phenomena.record: deixis: hin | her | none.

model.other: de:hereinkommen and de:hineingehen (both verb.enter), de:wohin, de:woher; fn.direction callouts.

phenomena.gap: A `deixis` feature on particles and verbs; more pairs (herauf/hinauf, heraus/hinaus) with the movement field.

phenomena.title: One meaning, several German words
phenomena.alsoNote: The particular splits are German; some are shared (kennen/wissen with fr connaître/savoir, es conocer/saber), others not.
phenomena.what: German divides several common meanings into separate words: when (wenn / als / wann), if (wenn / ob), because (weil / denn), to (zu / nach / in), at (an / bei / in / auf), from (aus / von), holiday (Urlaub / Ferien), hour (Stunde / Uhr), know (kennen / wissen). Each choice follows one question (past or not? whether or condition? kind of place?). The full list is in `distinctions`.

examples.text: Als ich jung war … – Wenn ich Zeit habe … – Wann kommst du?
Ich weiß nicht, ob er kommt. – Wenn es regnet, …
Ich bin aus Athen. – Ich komme von der Arbeit.

model.other: Every concept with two or more German words (88 concepts, 197 words) gives each word its contrast on one axis (D14 §4.5.2): conj.when als / wenn (time and repetition), prep.to zu / nach / an (kind of goal), verb.leave gehen / weggehen / verlassen (object and emphasis) …; the grammar pages have the decision procedures (askYourself).

phenomena.gap: The `sense_split` exercise (sort contexts into the words) is listed in §6.2 but not implemented.

phenomena.title: Homonyms and polysemy
phenomena.alsoNote: The particular homonyms and polysemous words are German.
phenomena.what: Many common words have meanings that are separate concepts: Bank (bank / bench), Schloss (castle / lock), Zug (train / move / draught), leicht (easy / light). Some differ in plural or gender (see the polysemy list).

examples.text: Ich gehe zur Bank. – Ich sitze auf der Bank.
Der Koffer ist leicht. – Die Aufgabe ist leicht.

phenomena.record: profile.senses – every distinct meaning with its concept (pending until taught), a nuance with “of”; the forms of one meaning in features (plurals, auxBySense, senseForms, homonyms).

model.other: Every sense of every German profile has a concept (pending when not taught) or “of” (D15); forms that belong to one meaning are in the parameters: plurals (Bänke), auxBySense (fahren), senseForms (möchte for mögen “would like”, das Ich, wessen, Ihr, einer / keiner standing alone, Frau and Schwester as titles, Bad in place names, -tag in Landtag), homonyms (das Morgen).

phenomena.gap: The `sense_pick` exercise (§6.2) is not implemented.

phenomena.title: Cognates, loans and false friends
phenomena.alsoNote: The cognates, loans and false friends are German; many are shared with nl, en, sv (Germanic) and with languages that borrowed from German.
phenomena.what: German shares many words with other languages, as inherited cognates (Haus, Buch, Mann) or as loans in both directions (Schule, Telefon, Computer; Rucksack, Kindergarten). Some look-alikes mean something else – false friends: Handy (mobile phone), also (so, therefore), Gift (poison), bekommen (to get), will (want), Chef (boss), eventuell (possibly), Apotheke (pharmacy). Which words are bridges and which are traps depends on the learner's languages.

examples.text: Haus – house; Buch – book; Mann – man

model.other: Profile pitfalls; callouts (also, Ich will); fn.overview forYou (Handy, Gift, bekommen). bridges.json does not exist. Every profile has an etymology with its source; fn.overview forYou notes.

phenomena.gap: bridges.json with kind falseFriend and the `cognate_bridge` exercise. bridges.json and the `etymology_link` / `cognate_bridge` exercises.

phenomena.title: Register: du-words and Sie-words, Oma and Großmutter
phenomena.what: Many meanings have a neutral or formal word and a colloquial one: Großmutter – Oma, Universität – Uni, auf Wiedersehen – tschüss, Guten Tag – hallo, Mobiltelefon – Handy. Choosing wrongly is a social mistake, not a grammar one.

model.other: Register on every sense and synonym; both words stored for a concept (greet.goodbye, family.grandmother, place.university).

phenomena.gap: The `register_pick` exercise is not implemented; transform Formality covers only du/Sie sentences.

phenomena.title: Collocations and noun–verb phrases (Funktionsverbgefüge)
phenomena.what: Verbs are mostly simple words; noun + light-verb phrases exist beside them, mainly in formal German: eine Frage stellen (ask), eine Entscheidung treffen (decide), Platz nehmen (sit down). The noun carries the meaning; the verb is fixed and learned with it.

model.other: Collocations required by the validator for NOUN/VERB/ADJ profiles.

phenomena.gap: The `collocation` exercise (§6.2) is not implemented.

phenomena.title: Kinship terms
phenomena.what: Kinship words do not say which side of the family: Onkel, Tante, Großvater, Großmutter are the same for the father's and the mother's side, and Onkel is also the aunt's husband. They mark sex (Bruder / Schwester, Cousin / Cousine) but not relative age. Oma / Opa are the everyday words, Großmutter / Großvater the neutral ones; Eltern and Großeltern are plural only.

examples.text: die Großeltern – der Großvater / der Opa

model.other: Lexicon fd.06 with the whole family field incl. register pairs (Opa/Großvater) and variants (Kusine).

phenomena.title: Siblings without age
phenomena.what: Bruder and Schwester say nothing about age; Geschwister means brothers and sisters together. Age is added with an adjective only when it matters: mein älterer Bruder (my older brother), meine kleine Schwester (my little sister).

examples.note: brothers and sisters, age not said

model.other: Comparison notes (D18): fn.have notes (zh, ja, hu, vi).

phenomena.title: du, ihr and Sie
phenomena.what: du (one person) and ihr (several) for family, friends, children and, increasingly, colleagues; Sie – capitalized, with the verb of ‘they’, for one or many – for adults you do not know well. Switching to du is offered by the older or higher-ranking person (das Du anbieten). The choice changes the pronoun, the possessive, the verb, the imperative and the greeting.

examples.text: Wie geht es dir? – Wie geht es Ihnen?
dein Buch – euer Buch – Ihr Buch

phenomena.record: features.address (PRON; DET.poss: informal | formal, or none) and features.formality (INTJ: informal | neutral | formal).

model.other: Lexemes de:du, de:ihr, de:Sie (pron.you.sg + pron.you.pl), de:dein, de:euer, de:Ihr.poss, three ‘how are you’ lexemes; bank variant Formality (11 sentences) with transform generators in 5 functions; V;IMP;FORM cell.

phenomena.title: No honorific forms or speech levels
phenomena.what: Politeness does not change verbs or nouns into honorific forms, and there are no speech levels. Respect is shown by the pronoun (Sie with the plural verb instead of du: Kommen Sie?), by Herr / Frau and titles, by Konjunktiv II (Könnten Sie …?) and by bitte. The verbs for the speaker and for the person addressed are the same words: essen, gehen, sagen for anyone.

examples.note: only the pronoun and its verb ending change

model.other: Comparison notes (D18): fn.overview, fn.pronoun.subject, fn.greetings and fn.imperative notes (ja, ko).

phenomena.title: The speaker's sex does not change the speech
phenomena.what: Men and women use the same words, endings and sentence-final forms; no verb or adjective agrees with the speaker's sex: Ich bin müde, Ich war krank for anyone. Only a noun about the speaker follows their sex (Ich bin Lehrer / Ich bin Lehrerin).

examples.text: Ich bin Lehrer. – Ich bin Lehrerin.
examples.note: only the noun for a person changes

model.other: Comparison notes (D18): fn.copula notes (hi, he: the speaker’s sex in the 1st person).

phenomena.title: Greetings by time of day and region
phenomena.alsoNote: The greetings, their register and regional forms (Grüß Gott, Moin, Grüezi, Mahlzeit) are German; greeting by time of day is widespread.
phenomena.what: Guten Morgen / Tag / Abend by the time of day, Gute Nacht only when parting late. Hallo and Tschüss go with du, Guten Tag and Auf Wiedersehen with Sie. Regions have their own: Grüß Gott and Servus in Bavaria and Austria, Moin in the north, Grüezi in Switzerland. At noon colleagues greet each other with Mahlzeit!, at table Guten Appetit!

examples.text: Guten Morgen! – Guten Tag! – Guten Abend! – Gute Nacht!

phenomena.record: region (variants) and register on greeting lexemes.

model.other: INTJ lexemes for the standard formulas; regional ones only in a callout of fn.greetings.

phenomena.gap: Regional greetings as lexemes (or variants with region); Guten Appetit / Mahlzeit with the meals.

phenomena.title: Modal particles: ja, doch, mal, denn, halt …
phenomena.alsoNote: Unstressed attitude particles in the middle of the clause: nl toch, maar, even, wel, eens; sv ju, väl, nog. Partly: ru же, ведь; pl przecież; ja, ko, yue sentence-final particles with similar functions in another position.
phenomena.what: Small unstressed words in the middle of the sentence add the speaker's attitude and stance towards what is said: ja (as we both know), doch (come on / after all), mal (just, softens a request), denn (in questions: interest, impatience), halt / eben (that's how it is), schon (surely), wohl (presumably – an inference), vielleicht (amazement). They are hard to translate but make German sound natural.

model.other: Every particle use is its own meaning with a concept (D15): ja s2 part.afterall, doch s3 part.urge, denn s2 part.then, auch s3 part.sure, aber s2 / vielleicht s3 adv.truly; fn.imperative ‘Softeners’ (bitte, mal, doch). mal, halt, eben, schon, wohl are not lexemes.

phenomena.gap: The missing particles as lexemes, and an exercise (which particle fits the situation).

phenomena.title: Polite requests
phenomena.what: A bare imperative can sound sharp; polite German uses bitte, Konjunktiv II (möchte, hätte gern, könnten Sie) and softeners (mal, vielleicht). Danke alone after an offer often means ‘no, thank you’.

model.other: möchte (de:mögen cells), bitte, softeners in fn.imperative, the danke trap in fn.greetings.

phenomena.gap: hätte gern / könnten / würden (cr.05).

phenomena.title: Herr, Frau and titles
phenomena.alsoNote: Herr/Frau + surname for every adult and academic titles in address are German (especially Austrian) conventions.
phenomena.what: Adults are addressed as Herr / Frau + surname with Sie; Frau is used for every woman whatever her marital status (Fräulein is obsolete). Academic titles are part of the address: Frau Dr. Weber.

examples.text: Herr Müller, kommen Sie bitte herein!

model.other: de:Frau has the sense ‘Mrs, Ms – title before a surname’; Herr is not a course word.

phenomena.gap: Herr (a weak noun: Herrn) as a lexeme in fd.02 and address sentences in the bank.

phenomena.title: Germany, Austria, Switzerland: one language, three standards
phenomena.alsoNote: The particular standards and dialects are German. Several national standards are familiar from en, es, pt, fr, nl; a spoken-dialect / written-standard split like Swiss German resembles the diglossia of ar.
phenomena.what: German has three national standards with their own words and spellings (Austrian Jänner, Paradeiser, Erdapfel; Swiss ss for ß, Rüebli) and strong regional dialects. In Germany and Austria the standard is both written and spoken, with regional colouring, so writing and educated speech are one language. German-speaking Switzerland is different: everyday speech is Swiss German dialect, and Standard German is written and used in formal settings – a diglossia in that region.

model.other: variants on 27 nouns (Jänner, Feber, Paradeiser, Erdapfel, Karfiol, Rüebli …); fn.overview ‘Standard variety’ fact.

phenomena.gap: variants exist only on nouns (not on greetings, verbs, particles); typed answers do not accept variants; region-wide spelling (CH ss) is not a rule; Swiss diglossia not explained.

phenomena.title: Meals and food culture
phenomena.alsoNote: The meals and food customs are German-speaking culture.
phenomena.what: Frühstück, Mittagessen, Abendessen – in many families the evening meal is a cold one (Abendbrot); Kaffee und Kuchen is an afternoon meal of its own, especially on Sundays. Mahlzeit! greets colleagues at noon, Guten Appetit! starts a meal.

examples.note: a cold supper of bread (northern and eastern word)

model.other: Profile sense of de:Kaffee (‘afternoon coffee and cake’) and of de:Mittag (lunch).

phenomena.gap: Culture notes on the meal words (fd.07).

phenomena.title: Week, date and clock conventions
phenomena.what: The Gregorian calendar is the only one in use. Weekday names come from heavenly bodies and old gods (Sonntag sun, Montag moon, Dienstag, Donnerstag Donar, Freitag Frija), except Mittwoch (mid-week) and Samstag / Sonnabend; the months have Latin names (Januar … Dezember; Austrian Jänner). The week starts on Monday and weeks are numbered (KW 41 = Kalenderwoche 41); dates are day.month.year (08.10.2026); written and official times use the 24-hour clock (um 20 Uhr), while speech often uses 12 hours (um acht Uhr abends).

examples.text: um 20 Uhr – um acht Uhr abends

model.other: fn.ordinals (cr.04) teaches dates (der achte Oktober, am achten Oktober, 08.10.2026, years read as neunzehnhundertneunzig) and the 24-hour clock.

phenomena.gap: No `date` / `clock` exercise; calendar weeks (KW) are not taught.

phenomena.title: Number words: einundzwanzig, eins / ein, Milliarde
phenomena.what: Counting is decimal. Between the tens German says the unit first, joined with und, in one word: 21 = einundzwanzig (‘one-and-twenty’); above a hundred the order is hundreds – units – tens (365 dreihundertfünfundsechzig). Long numbers are written as one word. sechs and sieben lose letters in sechzehn, sechzig, siebzehn, siebzig. ‘One’ is eins when counting but the declined article ein before a noun – the only cardinal that agrees with its noun; on the phone zwei becomes zwo. Large numbers go by thousands and follow the long scale: Million = 10⁶, Milliarde = 10⁹, Billion = 10¹².

examples.note: s dropped only in sechzehn, sechzig

NOUN.title: gender
NOUN.why: Chooses the article (der / die / das), the pronoun and the adjective endings; learned with every noun. Plural-only nouns (class plt) have none.

NOUN.title: plural, per meaning
NOUN.why: The plural is not predictable and is learned with the noun; a meaning may have its own plural (Banken / Bänke) or none (das Land = the countryside). A meaning left out of every item has no plural. none: mass nouns (class sgt) and plural-only nouns (class plt).

NOUN.title: singular declension
NOUN.why: strong: des Tisches, dem Tisch (-(e)s in the genitive); weak (n-declension): den / dem / des Jungen; mixed: des Namens, den Namen; feminine: no ending in the singular; adjectival: declined like an adjective (der Verwandte, ein Verwandter).

NOUN.title: compound parts
NOUN.why: The last part (head) gives the gender and the plural, the parts before it narrow the meaning; linker = the joining element (Blume-n-kohl, Geburt-s-tag) or “−e” when the first part loses its final e (Kirsch-tomate). A verb as modifier appears as its stem (wohnen → Wohnzimmer). none: a simple or derived word, or two separate words.

NOUN.title: same form, other gender
NOUN.why: der Junge (boy) / das Junge (young animal): the article alone tells two words apart. senses: when the other gender belongs to a meaning of this word.

NOUN.title: forms of one meaning
NOUN.why: A meaning used in a form or construction of its own besides its plural (Frau as a title: Frau Weber, never plural; Bad in place names: in Bad Ems). none: every meaning uses the same forms.

VERB.title: principal parts
VERB.why: infinitive – 3rd person singular present – 3rd person singular Präteritum – Partizip II: the four forms every learner memorizes (separable verbs with the particle in place: kommt an, kam an, angekommen).

VERB.title: conjugation class
VERB.why: weak: -te, ge-…-t (kaufen); strong: vowel change, ge-…-en (trinken – trank – getrunken); mixed: vowel change with weak endings (rennen – rannte – gerannt); modal: modal verbs (mögen, wollen); irregular: sein, haben.

VERB.title: vowel change in the present (du / er)
VERB.why: essen → du isst, fahren → du fährst, laufen → du läufst; decides the du-forms and the du-imperative (iss!).

VERB.title: perfect auxiliary
VERB.why: sein for movement and change of state (ist gegangen), haben for the rest; both: it depends on the meaning or on a direct object (hat das Auto gefahren / ist nach Berlin gefahren) – see auxBySense.

VERB.title: auxiliary per meaning
VERB.why: For verbs with aux “both”: which meaning (or construction) takes which auxiliary. none: one auxiliary for every meaning.

VERB.title: separable particle
VERB.why: The stressed particle goes to the end of the clause (Ich komme morgen an), ge- and zu go inside it (angekommen, anzukommen).

VERB.title: inseparable prefix
VERB.why: An unstressed prefix that never separates and takes no ge- in the participle (verlassen – verlassen).

VERB.title: objects and complements, per meaning
VERB.why: The case of each object (helfen + DAT, kaufen + ACC (+ DAT)), a preposition the verb chooses (warten auf + ACC), or a predicative nominative (Ich heiße Anna). none: the verb takes no object in any meaning.

VERB.title: reflexive use, per meaning
VERB.why: A meaning that needs the reflexive pronoun (sich verlassen auf: ich verlasse mich). none: no reflexive meaning.

VERB.title: manner of motion
VERB.why: German chooses the verb by how one moves: gehen (on foot), fahren (in a vehicle), fliegen (by air); kommen, reisen say nothing about it.

VERB.title: forms of one meaning
VERB.why: A meaning that uses forms of its own (mögen “would like” → möchte, möchtest …). none: every meaning uses the same forms.

ADJ.title: comparison
ADJ.why: regular: klein – kleiner – am kleinsten; umlaut: alt – älter – am ältesten; irregular: gut – besser – am besten, hoch – höher; not compared: rosa, lila. The forms are in ADJ;CMPR and ADJ;SPRL.

ADJ.title: stem before an ending
ADJ.why: Some adjectives change before an ending: hoch → hoh- (ein hoher Turm), dunkel → dunkl-, teuer → teur-. none: the ending is added to the base form (or the word takes no endings).

ADV.title: comparative and superlative
ADV.why: Some adverbs compare: oft – öfter – am öftesten, bald – eher – am ehesten. none: not compared (or itself a comparative / superlative form).

ADP.title: case, per meaning
ADP.why: Every preposition decides the case of its noun; the two-way prepositions (in, an, auf …) take the dative for where? and the accusative for where to?, and some meanings take only one (über “about” + ACC, am Montag + DAT). A meaning that is not prepositional (zu “too”, auf “open”) is in no item. A contraction (im, zum) states the case of its article; senses: omitted.

ADP.title: merged with the article
ADP.why: in + dem = im, zu + der = zur; some merged forms are colloquial (unterm, übers). none: no merged forms, or the word is itself a merged form.

DET.title: adjective endings after it
DET.why: der-words → weak endings (der gute Wein), ein-words → mixed (ein guter Wein), words that show no case themselves → strong (viel guter Wein, einige gute Freunde).

DET.title: addressee
DET.why: dein / euer (du, ihr) or Ihr (Sie). none: the owner is not the person spoken to.

DET.title: forms of one meaning
DET.why: A meaning with forms of its own (ein standing alone → einer, eine, eins). none: every meaning uses the same forms.

PRON.title: addressee
PRON.why: du / ihr (informal) or Sie (formal). none: not a pronoun of address.

PRON.title: what it refers to
PRON.why: er / sie / es refer to things as well, by the gender of the noun (der Tisch → er); wer asks for persons, was for things.

PRON.title: forms of one meaning
PRON.why: A meaning with forms of its own (das Ich, die Ichs; Ihr written with a capital). none: every meaning uses the same forms.

NUM.title: ordinal (der …)
NUM.why: The ordinal adjective: -te up to 19 (der zweite), -ste from 20 (der zwanzigste); irregular erste, dritte, siebte (also siebente), achte.

SCONJ.title: position of the finite verb
values: at the end of its clause
SCONJ.why: A subordinating conjunction sends the finite verb to the end of its clause (…, weil ich Hunger habe).

CCONJ.title: effect on word order
CCONJ.why: und, oder, aber, denn stand before the clause and change nothing (…, denn ich habe Hunger); weder / noch take the first place, so the verb follows them (Weder hat er angerufen, noch …).

INTJ.title: formality
INTJ.why: Which situations the formula fits: informal (friends, family: hallo, tschüss), formal (strangers, customers: guten Tag, auf Wiedersehen, wie geht es Ihnen), neutral (both).
